description: INY_NASA brings together experts in Data Engineering, AI, and Software Engineering. We build innovative solutions by combining advanced data pipelines, AI, and strong coding skills to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS wildfire hotspot data. Join us to turn NASA satellite data into actionable insights! 🌍🛰️ We’re looking for GIS/Remote Sensing specialists, data scientists, and visualization developers to strengthen our team.
summary:
Veille Feux is a web application that brings NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS and VIIRS together in one interactive platform. Users can explore recent detections on a global map, filter by sensor and time period, inspect individual observations, and analyze imported historical data with seasonal calendars and year-to-year comparisons.

To help users anticipate periods that may deserve closer monitoring, the app compares upcoming dates with sampled observations from the same month in the previous year, in the same geographic cell and from the same sensor. It also provides forecast weather and an illustrative wind corridor for selected detections. These features offer exploratory context, not guaranteed fire predictions or operational fire-spread forecasts.

By making current and historical satellite observations easier to explore, Veille Feux helps researchers, land managers, and response teams identify patterns and prioritize monitoring, while clearly communicating uncertainty and data limitations.
details:
Project Details

Veille Feux, developed by team INY_NASA, is a web application for exploring active-fire detections from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors. It brings recent FIRMS observations together on an interactive map, where users can filter by sensor and time period, inspect detection details, and focus on a selected area. Large map requests are divided into smaller areas to make live data loading more reliable.

The application also supports historical exploration. Users can import FIRMS CSV archives and examine activity by month, year, sensor, and area. An exploratory notifications view compares recent detections with sampled observations from the same month one year earlier, in the same one-degree geographic cell and from the same sensor. This historical reference can help highlight periods or locations for closer monitoring, but it does not predict that a fire will occur. For a selected detection, users can also view weather forecasts and an illustrative wind corridor for up to 72 hours; this is exploratory context, not an operational fire-spread forecast.

Veille Feux aims to make satellite observations easier to explore and interpret for researchers, land managers, and response teams. By bringing current detections and historical patterns into one interface, it can help users identify recurring seasonal activity and decide where further attention may be useful.

The project was built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Node.js, using Leaflet for mapping and a PostgreSQL-backed service for historical sampling and indexing. It uses NASA FIRMS for fire detections, Open-Meteo for weather forecasts and place search, and OpenStreetMap for map tiles. No specialized hardware is required.

A key design consideration was scientific reliability: MODIS and VIIRS have different resolutions, sensitivities, and overpass times, so the app preserves sensor identity rather than treating their measurements as interchangeable. It also distinguishes detections from unique fires, makes data limitations and missing coverage explicit, and stores user-imported historical files locally in the browser.
